claim: Homologous recombination (HR) preserves genomic stability by repairing double-strand DNA breaks.
source: Homologous recombination (HR) preserves genomic stability by repairing double-strand DNA breaks and ensuring efficient DNA replication.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by the citation context of the manuscript.

claim: Homologous recombination ensures efficient DNA replication.
source: Homologous recombination (HR) preserves genomic stability by repairing double-strand DNA breaks and ensuring efficient DNA replication.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the manuscript (Chakraborty et al., 2023; Triplett et al., 2024).

claim: The strand-exchange reaction in HR takes place within a three-stranded synapsis where a RAD51 nucleoprotein filament binds to donor DNA.
source: Central to HR is the strand-exchange reaction taking place within the three-stranded synapsis wherein a RAD51 nucleoprotein filament binds to a donor DNA.
evidence: This is a fundamental concept in HR supported by the literature and the structural data presented.

claim: The cryoEM structure of the RAD51 D-loop captures the synaptic state when the filament has become tightly bound to donor DNA.
source: Here, we present the cryoEM structure of a displacement loop of human RAD51 that captures the synaptic state when the filament has become tightly bound to the donor DNA.
evidence: This is directly supported by the structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The structure elucidates the mechanism of strand exchange by RAD51, including filament engagement with donor DNA, strand invasion and pairing, capture of the non-complementary strand, and polarity of the reaction.
source: The structure elucidates the mechanism of strand exchange by RAD51, including the filament engagement with the donor DNA, the strand invasion and pairing with the complementary sequence of the donor DNA, the capture of the non-complementary strand and the polarity of the strand-exchange reaction.
evidence: This is supported by the detailed structural analysis presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: HR deficiency causes genetic instability that predisposes to cancer.
source: HR deficiency causes genetic instability that predisposes to cancer (Triplett et al., 2024; Prakash et al., 2015; Matos-Rodrigues et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations in the manuscript.

claim: Synthetic lethality of HR with other DNA repair pathways is exploited to induce cancer cell death in therapy.
source: and its synthetic lethality with other DNA repair pathways is exploited to induce cancer cell death in therapy (Lord and Ashworth, 2017; Dibitetto et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to therapeutic applications.

claim: In eukaryotic cells, the reaction of HR is performed by RAD51.
source: In eukaryotic cells, the reaction of HR is performed by RAD51 (Baumann et al., 1996; Sung, 1994)
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational work on RAD51.

claim: RAD51 is a member of a highly conserved family of ATPases that includes bacterial RecA and archaeal RadA.
source: In eukaryotic cells, the reaction of HR is performed by RAD51 (Baumann et al., 1996; Sung, 1994), a member of a highly conserved family of ATPases that includes bacterial RecA and archaeal RadA (Lin et al., 2006; Chintapalli et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to comparative studies.

claim: RAD51 polymerises on single-stranded DNA overhangs that form upon long-range resection of DNA ends.
source: RAD51 polymerises on the single-stranded (ss) DNA overhangs that form upon long-range resection of DNA ends (Cejka and Symington, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to work on DNA end resection.

claim: The RAD51 nucleoprotein filament invades the donor DNA duplex and searches for sequence homology within a three-stranded synaptic filament intermediate.
source: The RAD51 nucleoprotein filament invades the donor DNA duplex and searches for sequence homology within a three-stranded synaptic filament intermediate (Renkawitz et al., 2014; Greene, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to mechanistic studies.

claim: When homology is found, the invading strand becomes stably paired to the complementary sequence of the donor DNA, yielding a displacement loop (D-loop).
source: When homology is found, the invading strand of the filament becomes stably paired to the complementary sequence of the donor DNA, yielding a structure known as a displacement loop (D-loop) (Shibata et al., 1979; Jain et al., 1995; Piazza et al., 2019; Figure 1A)
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: RAD51 can catalyse the biochemical reaction of strand exchange independently.
source: Although cellular HR is controlled by a complex network of recombination mediators such as BRCA2 (Bell et al., 2023), the RAD51 paralogues (Greenhough et al., 2023; Taylor et al., 2015; Rawal et al., 2023), and FIGNL1 (Ito et al., 2023; Carver et al., 2025), RAD51 can catalyse the biochemical reaction of strand exchange independently.
evidence: This is stated as a fact with supporting citations for the regulatory context.

claim: The final single-particle reconstruction comprises a nucleoprotein filament of 9 RAD51 protomers and 26 nucleotides of ssDNA, bound to a dsDNA containing a central bubble region flanked by 15- and 16-bp-long segments.
source: The final single-particle reconstruction based on 102,596 particles comprises a nucleoprotein filament of 9 RAD51 protomers and 26 nucleotides of ssDNA, bound to a dsDNA containing the central bubble region flanked by 15- and 16-bp-long segments of donor DNA.
evidence: This is directly supported by the cryoEM reconstruction data.

claim: The cryoEM map ranges in resolution between 2.5 Å and 2.9 Å for the homologous pairing region and 3 Å and 6 Å for the flanking dsDNA arms.
source: The cryoEM map ranges in resolution between 2.5 Å and 2.9 Å for the homologous pairing region of the D-loop and 3 Å and 6 Å for the flanking dsDNA arms (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly supported by the resolution analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In the D-loop structure, RAD51 maintains the right-handed helical arrangement of protomers observed in pre- and post-synaptic filaments.
source: In the D-loop structure, RAD51 maintains the right-handed helical arrangement of protomers observed in pre- and post-synaptic filaments (Short et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by comparison with previously published structures.

claim: The D-loop structure shows a slightly compressed pitch relative to the pre-synaptic filament.
source: In the D-loop structure, RAD51 maintains the right-handed helical arrangement of protomers observed in pre- and post-synaptic filaments (Short et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2017), with the same helical twist and a slightly compressed pitch relative to the pre-synaptic filament (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 4A, and Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Continuous density for the exchanged strand connects the arms of the donor DNA.
source: Continuous density for the exchanged strand (es), that becomes excluded upon homologous pairing of the invading strand (is) with the complementary strand (cs) of the donor DNA, connects the arms of the donor DNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryoEM density map shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: The filament-bound exchanged strand DNA follows a peripheral path along the filament groove that runs parallel to the invading strand DNA.
source: The filament-bound esDNA follows a peripheral path along the filament groove that runs parallel to the isDNA (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The conformation of the duplex formed by pairing of the invading strand and complementary strand resembles closely that of the dsDNA in the post-synaptic filament.
source: The conformation of the duplex formed by pairing of the isDNA and csDNA strands resembles closely that of the dsDNA in the post-synaptic filament (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C; Xu et al., 2017; Appleby et al., 2023a)
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C and citations.

claim: Sharp bends occur at the junctions where the donor DNA enters and exits the filament.
source: The conformation of the duplex formed by pairing of the isDNA and csDNA strands resembles closely that of the dsDNA in the post-synaptic filament (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C; Xu et al., 2017; Appleby et al., 2023a), with sharp bends at the junctions where the donor DNA enters and exits the filament (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figures 1C and D.

claim: The 5'-arm of the donor DNA is almost perpendicular to the filament axis with its filament-proximal end pointing slightly towards the 3'-end of the filament (3'-tilt).
source: the dsDNA arm closer to the 5'-end of the filament, hereinafter referred to as the 5'-arm, is almost perpendicular to the filament axis, with its filament-proximal end pointing slightly towards the 3'-end of the filament (3'-tilt)
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure and quantified in Figure 1—figure supplement 4D.

claim: The 3'-arm of the donor DNA exhibits a more pronounced tilt towards the 5'-end of the ssDNA (5'-tilt).
source: whereas the dsDNA arm closer to the 3'-end of the filament, hereinafter referred to as the 3'-arm, exhibits a more pronounced tilt in the opposite direction, towards the 5'-end of the ssDNA (5'-tilt) (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 4D.

claim: The opposite tilt of the donor arms favours their connection via the exchanged strand DNA in the D-loop structure.
source: The opposite tilt of the donor arms favours their connection via the esDNA strand in the D-loop structure.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural arrangement observed.

claim: A continuous span of 10 base-pair interactions is present between the invading strand DNA and complementary strand DNA.
source: A continuous span of 10 base-pair interactions is present between the isDNA and csDNA (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 5A.

claim: Base pairing includes the entirety of the complementary strand DNA sequence designed to be homologous to the invading strand, with the exception of G26cs.
source: Base pairing includes the entirety of the csDNA sequence designed to be homologous to the invading strand, with the exception of G26cs (Figure 1E and F and Figure 1—figure supplement 5A)
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figures 1E, F and Figure 1—figure supplement 5A.

claim: G26cs adopts a minor-occupancy conformation in the direction of C8 in the invading strand but too distant for Watson-Crick hydrogen bonding.
source: its guanine base adopts a minor-occupancy conformation in the direction of C8 in the isDNA but too distant for Watson-Crick hydrogen bonding, while the predominant conformation is pointing away (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B.

claim: Base pairing is fully maintained in the transition between the complementary strand:invading strand duplex and the flanking arms of the donor DNA, with the exception of G26cs.
source: Base pairing is fully maintained in the transition between the csDNA:isDNA duplex and the flanking arms of the donor DNA (Figure 1F and G), with the exception of the aforementioned G26cs.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figures 1F and G.

claim: An additional, mismatched base pair is formed at the junction of the complementary strand:invading strand duplex with the 3'-arm of the donor DNA, where T18is becomes base paired with G16cs.
source: Unexpectedly, an additional, mismatched base pair is formed at the junction of the csDNA:isDNA duplex with the 3'-arm of the donor DNA, where T18is becomes base paired with G16cs (Figure 1E, G and Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figures 1E, G and Figure 1—figure supplement 5A.

claim: Factors in addition to hydrogen-bonding potential contribute to determining pairing between the donor DNA and the invading strand of the filament.
source: This observation indicates that factors in addition to hydrogen-bonding potential contribute to determining pairing between the donor DNA and the invading strand of the filament.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of the mismatched base pair and the unrealized G26cs:C8is pair.

claim: RAD51 loops L1 and L2 mediate DNA binding, with prominent roles for amino acids L1 R235 and L2 V273 in partitioning filament DNA into nucleotide triplets.
source: Biochemical and structural analyses of pre- and post-synaptic filaments have revealed that RAD51 loops L1 and L2 mediate DNA binding, with prominent roles for amino acids L1 R235 and L2 V273 in partitioning filament DNA into nucleotide triplets (Xu et al., 2017; Matsuo et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural and biochemical studies.

claim: L2 residues Q272 to P283 remained disordered in pre- and post-synaptic filament structures.
source: However, L2 residues Q272 to P283 remained disordered in these filament structures (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated as a fact about previous structures, with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: In the D-loop structure, the L2 sequences of four contiguous RAD51 protomers (E, F, G, and H) have become ordered and traceable in the density map.
source: In our D-loop structure, the L2 sequences of four contiguous RAD51 protomers – E, F, G, and H (Figure 2B) – have become ordered and traceable in the density map, folding in random-coil conformation with 310-helix elements.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryoEM density map.

claim: Filamentous RAD51 achieves strand separation by sequential L2-loop insertion of adjacent RAD51 protomers between the strands of the donor DNA.
source: The structure shows that filamentous RAD51 achieves strand separation by sequential L2-loop insertion of adjacent RAD51 protomers between the strands of the donor DNA (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figures 2C and D.

claim: Insertion of the RAD51-H L2 loop at the 5'-arm junction causes a drastic widening of the minor groove.
source: Insertion of the RAD51-H L2 loop at the 5'-arm junction causes a drastic widening of the minor groove, progressing to full separation of the complementary and exchanged strands upon L2-loop insertion by RAD51-G (Figure 2C, D, G, and H).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figures 2C, D, G, and H.

claim: Donor DNA unwinding by RAD51-H and -G exposes a continuous complementary strand DNA stretch of five nucleotides for homologous pairing.
source: In total, donor DNA unwinding by RAD51-H and -G exposes a continuous csDNA stretch of five nucleotides for homologous pairing: A22-C25 of csDNA base pair with G9-T12 of isDNA
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure and described in the text.

claim: Successive L2-loop insertions extend the unwinding of donor DNA, with each insertion exposing a triplet of complementary strand DNA nucleotides for homology pairing with the invading strand.
source: Successive L2-loop insertions extend the unwinding of donor DNA, with each insertion exposing a triplet of csDNA nucleotides for homology pairing with the invading strand (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figure 2C.

claim: After completion of homologous pairing, the strands of the donor DNA rejoin in double-helical form at the 3'-arm junction.
source: After completion of homologous pairing, the strands of the donor DNA rejoin in double-helical form at the 3'-arm junction (Figures 1G and 2C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figures 1G and 2C.

claim: The L2 loop acts as a physical spacer, directly separating the unwound strands of the donor DNA.
source: The L2 loop acts as a physical spacer, directly separating the unwound strands of the donor DNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations of L2 loop insertion.

claim: The L2 loop sequence is dominated by hydrophobic amino acids that make extensive contacts with the phosphoribose backbone of the exchanged strand DNA.
source: Its sequence is dominated by hydrophobic amino acids (Figure 2A) that make extensive contacts with the phosphoribose backbone of the esDNA and culminate in stacking of F279's phenylalanine side chain against the last base pair of the 5'-arm duplex (RAD51-H) or the aromatic bases of nucleotides in the exchanged strand (RAD51-G, F, E) (Figure 2E–H).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figures 2A and 2E-H.

claim: The L2 loop displays a considerable degree of conformational heterogeneity.
source: The L2 loop displays a considerable degree of conformational heterogeneity, likely because each loop engages in both common and unique contacts with the DNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations of different L2 loop conformations.

claim: RAD51-H L2 initiates donor DNA unwinding by buttressing the F279 side chain against G27cs:C15is, the last base pair of the 5'-arm duplex.
source: RAD51-H L2 initiates donor DNA unwinding by buttressing the F279 side chain against G27cs:C15is, the last base pair of the 5'-arm duplex (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Contact with RAD51-E L2 does not alter the conformation of the 3'-arm, as its F279 side chain stacks against C26 of the exchanged strand.
source: Conversely, contact with RAD51-E L2 does not alter the conformation of the 3'-arm, as its F279 side chain stacks against C26 of the exchanged strand (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The asymmetric binding of RAD51-H and -E L2 loops at the boundaries suggests that strand invasion and pairing follows a preferred direction.
source: The asymmetric binding of RAD51-H and -E L2 loops at the boundaries between the arms of the donor DNA and the three-stranded synaptic DNA suggests that strand invasion and pairing follows a preferred direction.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations of asymmetric L2 loop binding.

claim: Invasion by filament DNA likely begins at the 3'-end of the homology region in the complementary strand of the donor DNA and extends in the 5'-direction.
source: Thus, invasion by filament DNA likely begins at the 3'-end of the homology region in the complementary strand of the donor DNA and extends in the 5'-direction, as incrementally more nucleotides of csDNA are exposed by L2-loop insertions and become available for homologous pairing.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations and the mechanism of L2 loop insertion.

claim: The exchanged strand DNA is sequestered in a basic channel running parallel to the ssDNA-binding groove of the RAD51 nucleoprotein filament.
source: The structure of the D-loop shows that the esDNA is sequestered in a basic channel running parallel to the ssDNA-binding groove of the RAD51 nucleoprotein filament (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figures 3A and B.

claim: One side of the exchanged strand DNA-binding channel is formed by RAD51 residues 303–313, that fold in a beta hairpin on the inside of the filament groove.
source: One side of the channel is formed by RAD51 residues 303–313 (Figure 3C), that fold in a beta hairpin on the inside of the filament groove
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The opposite side of the exchanged strand DNA-binding channel is formed by the C-terminal half of the L2-loop sequence.
source: whereas the opposite side is formed by the C-terminal half of the L2-loop sequence (Figure 3B and D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figures 3B and D.

claim: In the filament, the beta hairpins of successive protomers align to generate a continuous ssDNA-binding stripe.
source: In the filament, the beta hairpins of successive protomers align to generate a continuous ssDNA-binding stripe (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The exchanged strand DNA is bound in the basic channel so that its aromatic bases remain largely exposed to solvent whereas the phosphodiester backbone faces the protein.
source: The esDNA is bound in the basic channel so that its aromatic bases remain largely exposed to solvent whereas the phosphodiester backbone faces the protein (Figure 3B and D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figures 3B and D.

claim: Three adjacent RAD51 protomers (F, G, and H) engage the exchanged strand in the D-loop.
source: Three adjacent RAD51 protomers – F, G, and H – engage the exchanged strand in the D-loop (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The majority of contacts between RAD51 and exchanged strand DNA comprise charged interactions between four invariant RAD51 residues R303, K304, R306, and K313 and the phosphate groups of the exchanged strand DNA.
source: The majority of contacts comprise charged interactions between four invariant RAD51 residues R303, K304, R306, and K313 and the phosphate groups of the esDNA (Figure 3E–G).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figures 3E-G.

claim: R306 is part of a GRG motif at the tip of the beta hairpin that comes into close contact with the phosphoribose backbone of the exchanged strand DNA and makes stacking interactions with the aromatic bases of nucleotides A19es and T25es in RAD51-H and -G.
source: In addition to the electrostatic interactions, R306 is part of a GRG motif at the tip of the beta hairpin that comes into close contact with the phosphoribose backbone of the esDNA and makes stacking interactions with the aromatic bases of nucleotides A19es and T25es in RAD51-H and -G, respectively (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figures 3E and F.

claim: The interaction of the 305-GRG-307 motif with exchanged strand DNA resembles that of L1-loop 234-GRG-236 with complementary strand DNA in the homologous duplex of the D-loop.
source: The interaction of the 305-GRG-307 motif with esDNA resembles that of L1-loop 234-GRG-236 with csDNA in the homologous duplex of the D-loop.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of the structural features.

claim: RAD51-G makes the most extensive set of contacts with exchanged strand DNA, spanning five nucleotides from A21es to T25es, involving all four basic residues R303, K304, R306, and K313.
source: Of the three RAD51 protomers F, G, and H that bind the esDNA, RAD51-G makes the most extensive set of contacts, spanning five nucleotides, from A21es to T25es, involving all four basic residues R303, K304, R306, and K313 (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figure 3F.

claim: RAD51-H contacts four nucleotides from A17es to A20es with R303, K304, and 305-GRG-307.
source: RAD51-H contacts four nucleotides, from A17es to A20es, with R303, K304, and 305-GRG-307 (Figure 3E)
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figure 3E.

claim: RAD51-F makes a single long-range interaction between K313 and T25es.
source: whereas RAD51-F makes a single long-range interaction between K313 and T25es (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The filament interacts with 9 of the 11 nucleotides of unpaired exchanged strand DNA via contiguous interactions of the two RAD51 protomers G and H (5 and 4 nt, respectively).
source: In total, the filament interacts with 9 of the 11 nucleotides of unpaired esDNA via contiguous interactions of the two RAD51 protomers G and H (5 and 4 nt, respectively).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure and summarized in the text.

claim: Donor DNA opening by L2-loop insertion progresses by exposure of three nucleotides per RAD51 protomer.
source: This compares with donor DNA opening by L2-loop insertion, which progresses by exposure of three nucleotides per RAD51 protomer.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure and described in the text.

claim: The nucleoprotein filament interacts with the double-stranded arms of the donor DNA via the N-terminal domains of RAD51 protomers A and D.
source: The D-loop structure shows that the nucleoprotein filament interacts with the double-stranded arms of the donor DNA via the N-terminal domains of RAD51 protomers A and D (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figures 4A and B.

claim: The DNA-binding interfaces of RAD51-A and -D NTDs differ significantly in the extent and mode of their engagement with the 3'- and 5'-arm duplexes.
source: Although the position of the RAD51-A and -D NTDs relative to the donor DNA is broadly similar, their DNA-binding interfaces differ significantly in the extent and mode of their engagement with the 3'- and 5'-arm duplexes, respectively.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure and described in the text.

claim: The RAD51-D NTD engages the minor groove of the 5'-arm DNA.
source: The RAD51-D NTD engages the minor groove of the 5'-arm DNA (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The association of RAD51-D NTD with 5'-arm is closer and more extensive than that of RAD51-A with the 3'-arm.
source: The association of RAD51-D NTD with 5'-arm is closer and more extensive than that of RAD51-A with the 3'-arm, and includes a direct hydrogen bond between the main-chain nitrogen of G65 and the phosphate group of T12 (Figure 4C and E).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figures 4C and E.

claim: RAD51-A NTD binds in the major groove of the 3'-arm DNA, using electrostatic interactions mediated by the same set of lysine residues as in RAD51-D.
source: In contrast, RAD51-A NTD binds in the major groove of the 3'-arm DNA, using electrostatic interactions mediated by the same set of lysine residues as in RAD51-D (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The interaction of the NTD with the arms of the donor DNA highlights a lack of direct contacts with the bases and the predominantly electrostatic nature of the association.
source: The interaction of the NTD with the arms of the donor DNA highlights a lack of direct contacts with the bases and the predominantly electrostatic nature of the association.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations of NTD-DNA interactions.

claim: Plasticity in the NTD-DNA interaction might be required for effective D-loop formation, as the direction at which the 3'-arm exits the filament is a function of the number of nucleotides involved in homologous pairing.
source: Such plasticity in the NTD-DNA interaction might be required for effective D-loop formation, as the direction at which the 3'-arm exits the filament upon D-loop formation is a function of the number of nucleotides involved in homologous pairing.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations and the mechanism of D-loop formation.

claim: All RAD51 mutants tested showed a moderate decrease in affinity for dsDNA, with the exception of K304.
source: All RAD51 mutants showed a moderate decrease in affinity for dsDNA, with the exception of K304 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is directly supported by the EMSA data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: All RAD51 mutants decreased the efficiency of the strand-exchange reaction, but with varying degrees of impairment.
source: The results of the strand-exchange assay revealed that all mutants decreased the efficiency of the reaction, but with varying degrees of impairment (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is directly supported by the strand-exchange assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The L2-loop F279A mutant showed a modest impact on strand exchange.
source: The L2-loop F279A showed a modest impact, in agreement with earlier findings (Matsuo et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by the strand-exchange assay data and citation to previous work.

claim: The exchanged strand DNA-capture mutants R303A, K304A, R306A, and K313A displayed a more pronounced effect on strand exchange than F279A.
source: whereas the esDNA-capture mutants R303A, K304A, R306A, and K313A displayed a more pronounced effect.
evidence: This is directly supported by the strand-exchange assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The NTD mutations showed the largest negative impact on strand exchange.
source: Notably, the NTD mutations showed the largest negative impact on strand exchange: the double lysine-to-alanine substitutions of K39, K40 and K70, K73 reduced strand exchange to a fraction of the yield for the wild-type protein.
evidence: This is directly supported by the strand-exchange assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Wild-type RAD51 filaments were capable of D-loop formation at the expected site on λ DNA.
source: Wild-type RAD51 filaments were capable of D-loop formation at the expected site, as assessed by kymograph and binding events analysis (Figure 5D and E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is directly supported by the single-molecule data shown in Figures 5D, E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Filaments of the KK39,40AA RAD51 double mutant failed to show measurable binding events at the expected λ DNA site.
source: In contrast, filaments of the KK39,40AA RAD51 double mutant failed to show measurable binding events; a fivefold increase in the concentration of the double mutant protein showed non-specific binding and no stable D-loop formation at the expected λ DNA site (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is directly supported by the single-molecule data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The biochemical behavior of exchanged strand DNA-capture site mutants agrees with the impaired D-loop formation of a yeast RAD51 protein bearing alanine mutations at amino acids corresponding to R130, K303, and K313 of human RAD51.
source: The biochemical behaviour of our esDNA-capture site mutants agrees with the impaired D-loop formation of a yeast RAD51 protein bearing alanine mutations at amino acids corresponding to R130, K303, and K313 of human RAD51 (Cloud et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with cited work on yeast RAD51.

claim: The close engagement of the RAD51-D NTD with the 5'-arm duplex, coupled to minor-groove widening by the RAD51-H L2 loop, indicates that synapsis formation starts by interaction of the filament with the 5'-arm of the donor DNA.
source: The close engagement of the RAD51-D NTD with the 5'-arm duplex, coupled to minor-groove widening by the RAD51-H L2 loop that initiates DNA unwinding, indicates that synapsis formation starts by interaction of the filament with the 5'-arm of the donor DNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations of NTD and L2 loop interactions.

claim: The interaction of the RAD51-A NTD with the 3'-arm is more limited than with the 5'-arm.
source: In comparison, the interaction of the RAD51-A NTD with the 3'-arm is more limited
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure and described in the text.

claim: Insertion of the L2 loop of RAD51-E does not remodel the proximal end of the 3'-arm duplex.
source: and insertion of the L2 loop of RAD51-E does not remodel the proximal end of the 3'-arm duplex.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure and described in the text.

claim: The first invading strand DNA:complementary strand DNA base pair formed at the 3'-arm junction is a T:G mismatch that is unlikely to stabilise the initial strand pairing.
source: Furthermore, the first isDNA:csDNA base pair formed at the 3'-arm junction is a T:G mismatch that is unlikely to stabilise the initial strand pairing.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure and inferred from the nature of the mismatch.

claim: RAD51-D NTD binding directs the donor duplex towards the filament groove, where L2-loop insertions by RAD51-H and -G initiate strand separation and capture of the exchanged strand.
source: In the model, RAD51-D NTD binding directs the donor duplex towards the filament groove, where L2-loop insertions by RAD51-H and -G initiate strand separation and capture of the exchanged strand.
evidence: This is part of the mechanistic model proposed based on structural observations.

claim: Initial donor DNA unwinding exposes five nucleotides of complementary strand DNA, of which four are available for pairing with the invading strand of the filament.
source: Such unwinding exposes five nucleotides of csDNA, of which four are available for pairing with the invading strand of the filament.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure and described in the text.

claim: Initial base pair formation in the presence of homology would drive further donor DNA unwinding by L2-loop insertions of RAD51-F and -E.
source: Initial base pair formation in the presence of homology would drive further donor DNA unwinding by L2-loop insertions of RAD51-F and -E
evidence: This is part of the mechanistic model proposed based on structural observations.

claim: Each L2-loop insertion exposes a triplet of complementary strand DNA nucleotides, in agreement with experimental evidence that homologous pairing progresses in triplet steps.
source: each insertion exposes a triplet of csDNA nucleotides, in agreement with experimental evidence that homologous pairing progresses in triplet steps (Qi et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the structural observations and citations to experimental evidence.

claim: Concomitant capture of the exchanged strand by RAD51-G after insertion of a third L2 loop by RAD51-F would lead to sequestration of nine exchanged strand DNA nucleotides, contributing to the formation of a stable synaptic intermediate.
source: Concomitant capture of the exchanged strand by RAD51-G after insertion of a third L2 loop by RAD51-F would lead to sequestration of nine esDNA nucleotides, contributing to the formation of a stable synaptic intermediate.
evidence: This is part of the mechanistic model proposed based on structural observations.

claim: Successful homology pairing drives the engagement of the 3'-arm of the donor dsDNA with the NTD of the RAD51 molecule three protomer positions away towards the 3'-end of the filament, completing D-loop formation.
source: Successful homology pairing drives the engagement of the 3'-arm of the donor dsDNA with the NTD of the RAD51 molecule three protomer positions away towards the 3'-end of the filament, completing D-loop formation.
evidence: This is part of the mechanistic model proposed based on structural observations.

claim: The observed plasticity in the interaction of the NTD with dsDNA would facilitate capture of the 3'-arm DNA emerging at slightly different angles from the filament axis, depending on the exact number of paired nucleotides.
source: The observed plasticity in the interaction of the NTD with dsDNA would facilitate capture of the 3'-arm DNA emerging at slightly different angles from the filament axis, depending on the exact number of paired nucleotides.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations of NTD-DNA interactions.

claim: The structural features of the RAD51 D-loop provide a strong indication that strand pairing and exchange begins at the 3'-end of the complementary strand in the donor DNA and progresses with 3'-to-5' polarity.
source: Overall, the structural features of the RAD51 D-loop provide a strong indication that strand pairing and exchange begins at the 3'-end of the complementary strand in the donor DNA and progresses with 3'-to-5' polarity (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observations and summarized in Figure 5F.

claim: The mechanism of unwinding of the 5'-arm prevents base pairing of the first available complementary strand DNA nucleotide (G26cs), likely due to physical constraints.
source: The observation of an unrealised base pair involving G26cs at the 3'-end of the unwound csDNA, which was designed to base pair with C8is, indicates that the mechanism of unwinding of the 5'-arm prevents base pairing of the first available csDNA nucleotide, likely due to physical constraints.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation of the unrealized base pair.

claim: The presence of three consecutive G:C base pairs in the 5'-arm duplex possibly acted as a GC clamp, preventing further unwinding to allow G26cs pairing.
source: Further unwinding of the 5'-arm to allow G26cs pairing was not observed, possibly because the presence of three consecutive G:C base pairs in the 5'-arm duplex acted as a GC clamp.
evidence: This is speculated based on the structural observations.

claim: T18is and G16cs do not form a 'wobble' base pair, indicating that fulfilment of hydrogen bonding potential is not critical.
source: Of note, T18is and G16cs do not form a 'wobble' base pair (Hunter et al., 1987), indicating that fulfilment of hydrogen bonding potential is not critical.
evidence: This is directly observed in the structure and compared with known base-pairing patterns.

claim: Mismatch pairing that completes a base-pair triplet might occur regardless of perfect homology, to achieve a full complement of base stacking and protein-DNA interactions with RAD51 L1 and L2 loops.
source: Rather, mismatch pairing that completes a base-pair triplet might occur regardless of perfect homology, to achieve a full complement of base stacking and protein-DNA interactions with RAD51 L1 and L2 loops.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation of the mismatch base pair.

claim: This observation provides a potential mechanism for how RAD51 can tolerate mismatches at certain positions of the homologous sequence during strand exchange.
source: This observation provides a potential mechanism for how RAD51 can tolerate mismatches at certain positions of the homologous sequence during strand exchange.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation of the mismatch base pair.

claim: The observed 3'-to-5' polarity of exchange of the complementary strand by RAD51 is opposite to the 5'-to-3' polarity of bacterial RecA.
source: The observed 3'-to-5' polarity of exchange of the complementary strand by RAD51 is opposite to the 5'-to-3' polarity of bacterial RecA (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), which was determined based on cryoEM structures of RecA D-loops (Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with RecA structures shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and citation.

claim: The different polarity of RAD51 and RecA follows from the opposite position occupied by their dsDNA-binding domains in the filament.
source: Comparison of RAD51 and RecA D-loop structures reveals that their different polarity follows from the opposite position occupied by their dsDNA-binding domains in the filament
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of RAD51 and RecA structures.

claim: In a vertically oriented filament with the 5'-end of the ssDNA at the top and the 3'-end at the bottom, the RAD51 NTDs line the bottom of the filament groove whereas the RecA CTDs hang from the top.
source: in a vertically oriented filament with the 5'-end of the ssDNA at the top and the 3'-end at the bottom, the RAD51 NTDs line the bottom of the filament groove whereas the RecA CTDs hang from the top (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structural comparison shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: The shared mode of minor-groove binding by RAD51-NTD and RecA-CTD and L2-loop insertion into the minor groove half a turn away leads naturally to opposite polarity in the progression of strand invasion and pairing.
source: The shared mode of minor-groove binding by RAD51-NTD and RecA-CTD and L2-loop insertion into the minor groove half a turn away leads naturally to opposite polarity in the progression of strand invasion and pairing with the complementary strand of the donor DNA.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of RAD51 and RecA structures.

claim: The available evidence suggests that the ability to perform DNA-strand exchange by members of the RecA-family of recombinases results from a process of convergent evolution.
source: Altogether, the available evidence suggests that the ability to perform DNA-strand exchange by members of the RecA-family of recombinases results from a process of convergent evolution (Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of RAD51 and RecA structures and evolutionary considerations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: An ancestral RecA-fold ATPase protein might first have evolved to bind ssDNA using the L1 and L2 loops, possibly as a means of protecting the exposed DNA template during DNA replication.
source: Thus, an ancestral RecA-fold ATPase protein might first have evolved to bind ssDNA using the L1 and L2 loops, possibly as a means of protecting the exposed DNA template during DNA replication.
evidence: This is speculated based on evolutionary considerations.

claim: Independent acquisition of dsDNA binding by RecA and RAD51 via incorporation of carboxy- and amino-terminal domains might have endowed these proteins with the ability to engage simultaneously ss- and dsDNA and catalyse the exchange of homologous DNA strands.
source: Independent acquisition of dsDNA binding by RecA and RAD51 via incorporation of carboxy- and amino-terminal domains, respectively, might have further endowed these proteins with the ability to engage simultaneously ss- and dsDNA and catalyse the exchange of homologous DNA strands.
evidence: This is speculated based on evolutionary considerations and structural comparisons.

claim: The cryoEM structure of the RAD51 D-loop was determined at 2.64 Å resolution.
source: yielding a structure of the D-loop at 2.64 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by the data processing workflow shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: A minimum length of eight homologous nucleotides is required for the formation of stable synaptic joints by RAD51.
source: Furthermore, single-molecule experiments have determined the kinetic parameters of filament nucleation and growth (Galletto et al., 2006; Candelli et al., 2014), have shown that a minimum length of eight homologous nucleotides is required for the formation of stable synaptic joints (Hsieh et al., 1992; Qi et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to single-molecule experiments.

claim: Homologous pairing by RAD51 takes place in steps of three nucleotides.
source: and that homologous pairing takes place in steps of three nucleotides (Ragunathan et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to single-molecule experiments.
